title: Choosing between table and layer breeds
subtitle: What drives breed performance and how to match breed to purpose.
excerpt: Layer breeds and table breeds are optimised for different outputs. A laying breed focuses energy on egg production; a table breed focuses energy on muscle growth. Dual-purpose breeds sit between the two but rarely match either specialist in its main role. Here is what distinguishes the three groups and what to consider for a small holding.
sourceNotes: Poultry Club of Great Britain, breed standards and breed information. BFREPA British Free Range Egg Producers Association, breed selection guidance. British Poultry Council, genetic breed categories.

glossaryTerms.definition: A commercial or semi-commercial laying bird produced by crossing two or more pure breeds selected for egg-laying traits. Hybrid layers typically produce 280–320 eggs per year in their first season, outperforming most pure breeds.

A chicken breed historically developed to produce acceptable quantities of both eggs and meat, such as Sussex, Rhode Island Red, and Dorking. Performance in both categories is lower than specialist breeds.

content.text: and a Cornish Cross table bird is about the same as the difference between a racing greyhound and a carthorse. Both are chickens, but selective pressure over many generations has pushed them in completely opposite directions. Trying to get your meat and all your eggs from the same bird involves accepting that you will have a middling version of both.

Commercial hybrid layers (Hy-Line, Lohmann Brown, Warren) convert feed into eggs very efficiently. A first-year hybrid layer produces 280 to 320 eggs on 120 to 130 g of feed per day. Pure-breed layers (Leghorn, Ancona, Welsummer) produce 160 to 220 eggs per year. Layer breeds carry little muscle mass; the carcass of a spent commercial layer is not economically worth processing, though it produces excellent stock.

Cornish Cross (Ross 308, Cobb 500) reach 2.5 to 3 kg dressed weight in 8 to 9 weeks at the cost of high feed consumption and active welfare management. Freedom rangers and slower-growing hybrids reach similar weights in 12 to 16 weeks on pasture at lower intensity. Pure table breeds (Dorking, Ixworth) grow more slowly still and are typically killed at 16 to 20 weeks for a smaller carcass.

like the Light Sussex or Rhode Island Red produces 180 to 220 eggs per year and a useful carcass (1.5 to 2 kg dressed) from the surplus cockerels at 20 to 24 weeks. For a smallholder who wants a single flock that supplies both eggs and an occasional table bird, this is a practical choice. The trade-off is clear: 30 to 40% fewer eggs than a hybrid layer, and 50% more growing time than a fast table bird.
What to consider for a small holding
If eggs are the priority, a small flock of 4 to 6 hybrid layers supplies a household with 5 to 6 eggs per bird per week in the first year. Replace birds at 2 to 3 years when production drops.
If you want a breed to breed from, you need a pure breed or a slow-growing commercial hybrid. Hybrid layers do not breed true.
If you want both eggs and meat from one flock, a dual-purpose pure breed is the right choice. Accept lower performance on both metrics and the longer growing time for table birds.
Temperament varies by breed. Leghorns and Mediterranean breeds are flighty; Sussex, Orpington, and Plymouth Rock are calm and handle handling well.
